title: V3-1 — Loads, Load Paths, and Why Shapes Fail Where They Do

concepts.title: Every pound finds the ground
concepts.mechanism: Every pound of weight in a building — its own structure, the people and furniture in it, the wind pushing on it — has to travel down an unbroken chain of members to the ground: roof to beam to column to footing to rock. This chain is the load path, and it only takes ONE broken or missing link for the whole thing to fail at that exact point — not gradually, but right where the road runs out. When someone proposes removing or moving a structural element, the real question is never 'does it look fine' — it's 'where does its load go now.'
concepts.mechanismPro: Trace the load path member by member and check the tributary area feeding each one; know where tension lives in the system (bottom of a simple beam, top of a cantilever) since that is where reinforcement and connections matter most.
concepts.hook: A bucket-brigade line passing water to a fire: it doesn't matter how strong every other person in line is if one person in the middle drops out — the water (the load) simply doesn't arrive.

applied.prompt: A renovation proposes removing a bearing wall in a single-family house to open the floor plan. What's the first question you ask?

options.label: Where does the load currently carried by that wall go once it's gone — what replaces it in the load path?
options.outcome: Right. This is the only question that actually matters; everything else (aesthetics, room size) is downstream of whether the load has somewhere to go.

options.label: Ask the contractor if it's 'load-bearing' and take their word for it
options.outcome: A contractor's field judgment is a start, but a load-bearing determination for a structural change should be verified by an engineer, not assumed from experience alone.

options.label: Remove it — it's just a wall, and the room will look better open
options.outcome: If that wall was carrying floor or roof load, removing it without a new path (a beam, transfer structure) means the load has nowhere to go — sagging, cracking, or worse.

applied.debrief: This is the foundational law the whole physics backbone builds on. The same question — 'where does the load go now' — reappears as M07's condo lobby column, V3-2's lateral wind path, and S8's pavement layers. Learn to ask it here and you'll ask it everywhere.

summary: Every pound in a building must travel to the ground, and the path it takes — roof → beam → column → footing → rock — fails at its weakest link. PLAIN: loads are travelers looking for the ground. PRO: trace the load path, check the tributary area, know where tension lives.

sections.heading: Load paths and tributary area
sections.body: PLAIN: Every pound — the concrete itself, the furniture, the wind — has to travel somewhere, and the only place it can finally rest is the ground. The path is the LOAD PATH, and the load always finds the weakest link. Tributary area: imagine the floor as a pizza held up by people below — each column carries the slice nearest it, halfway to every neighbor. Double the column spacing and each column's slice doubles, which is why 'can we just remove this column?' is never a small question: its whole slice must find a new home. PRO: 'Trace the load path' is the first thing an engineer does with any drawing; 'there's no load path for that' means something will break making one. 'That column's picking up about 400 square feet' — tributary area × load per sf = the force in the member; the sanity check that doesn't need the engineer's math.

sections.heading: Dead, live, environmental
sections.body: PLAIN: DEAD load is the building's own permanent weight — it never leaves (and it dominates: a 6-inch concrete slab weighs 75 psf before anyone stands on it). LIVE load comes and goes — people, furniture, a party. ENVIRONMENTAL loads are nature's additions — wind and flood here. Engineers design for unlucky combinations peaking together, with margins, because the day everything peaks at once is the day that matters. PRO: 'load combinations,' 'factored loads' — code multiplies loads up and strength down; 'designed for 40 psf live' is how capacity gets quoted. Residential live ~40 psf; balconies/assembly 60–100; concrete at 150 pcf.

sections.heading: Compression, tension, bending, shear, buckling
sections.body: PLAIN: Push together = compression (concrete loves it). Pull apart = tension (concrete hates it; steel carries it). BENDING is sneaky — bend a beam and its bottom stretches while its top squeezes simultaneously, which is why steel goes in the bottom at midspan. SHEAR is a scissors cut, worst right next to supports — that's why the little steel loops (stirrups) cluster near beam ends. BUCKLING is the drinking-straw trick: press down and it doesn't crush, it suddenly bows sideways — slender things fail by buckling long before their material gives up, which is why bracing exists and why an unbraced green block wall is dangerous with nothing on it. PRO: 'tension face,' 'stirrups at the supports,' 'slenderness,' 'brace it off' — and the field classic: a cantilever's tension is on TOP (it droops like a diving board), so a balcony's main steel is in the top of the slab, and a crew that chairs it low has quietly halved the balcony. (S3's rule, physics edition.)

quiz.teach: PLAIN: each column holds the slice of floor nearest to it. PRO: tributary area = spacing × spacing on a regular grid.
quiz.prompt: A retail tenant wants a column removed for open floor. Columns sit on a 20×20 ft grid with 150 psf total design load. What does the tributary math say the missing column was carrying?

choices.text: About 60,000 lb (400 sf × 150 psf) — a load that now needs a transfer beam engineered to walk it sideways to the neighbors, which is why you price that before sales hears 'yes'
choices.why: Correct. 20×20 = 400 sf tributary; ×150 psf = 60,000 lb = 30 tons looking for a new home. Transfer structures are real and expensive — that's the conversation.

choices.text: Little — the slab redistributes to the other columns naturally
choices.why: Slabs redistribute SOME load at the cost of overstressing spans never designed for it. 'Naturally' is doing illegal engineering in that sentence.

choices.text: Whatever the column's own weight was
choices.why: The column's self-weight is trivial; its JOB — the 400 sf slice above it — is the 30 tons in question.
The full analysis comes later; tributary area × load per sf is exactly the sanity-check arithmetic that tells you TODAY this is a big ask.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: the column was holding its slice of the pizza — remove the hand and the slice needs a new hand. PRO: 'tributary 400 sf at 150 psf, 60 kips to transfer — get the EOR to price the transfer beam before anyone promises the tenant.' (V3-1)

quiz.teach: A cantilever droops like a diving board — its TOP stretches.
quiz.prompt: The site super reports balcony top steel 'sitting a bit low' before a condo pour. Why is this a stop-the-pour call rather than a note?

choices.text: The balcony's tension is on TOP — capacity scales with how high the steel sits (effective depth); bars sagging low quietly convert the designed balcony into a much weaker one, and balcony collapses worldwide trace to exactly this
choices.why: Correct. Low top steel in a cantilever isn't a tolerance issue — it's a different, weaker structure. The pour makes it permanent; the stop costs a morning.

choices.text: It's cosmetic — concrete covers the bars either way
choices.why: Cover hides position; physics uses it. The invisible inch of lost effective depth is a visible fraction of lost strength.

choices.text: Only bottom steel position matters in slabs
choices.why: In SIMPLE spans, yes — the cantilever flips the rule. The flip is the classic field error and the reason this check has its own name on the hold-point script.

choices.text: The engineer can recalculate around it after the pour
choices.why: Recalculation after the pour discovers the deficiency; it can't add capacity. Chairs before concrete; math can't chair bars retroactively.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: the balcony pulls on top, so the metal must ride high — bars that sag were never doing the job. PRO: 'verify cantilever top steel at design height before every pour; quantify effective-depth loss if in doubt and hold.' (V3-1, S3)

quiz.teach: The drinking-straw demonstration: slender things bow sideways before they crush.
quiz.prompt: A truss maker offers longer spans with lighter chords. What question does buckling force you to ask?

choices.text: What bracing/bridging does the lighter chord require — slender members fail by bowing sideways long before material strength matters, so the bracing schedule IS the design
choices.why: Correct. Lighter and longer means more slender; slenderness fails by buckling; and buckling is prevented by bracing that must be installed, inspected, and never 'omitted for now.'

choices.text: Whether the lighter steel is weaker material
choices.why: Material strength barely enters — a slender strut at half its buckling length carries 4x. Geometry and bracing govern, not the mill certificate.

choices.text: Whether the price break is real
choices.why: Commercially fair, structurally beside the point — the truss can be cheaper AND fine, IF its bracing requirements travel with it to the field.
Their design assumes bracing your crews must install. The failure mode is the gap between the design's assumptions and the site's habits.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: press a straw — it bows, it doesn't crush; skinnier and longer bows sooner, unless held in the middle. PRO: 'lighter chords = tighter bridging/bracing schedule; the bracing goes on the inspection checklist or the span comes off the order.' (V3-1)

mathProblems.title: Tributary pizza problem
mathProblems.context: Column load = tributary area × total design load per sf. On a regular grid the tributary area is spacing × spacing — the sanity check every drawing review starts with.

decisionPoints.title: The open-floor request
decisionPoints.scenario: The retail leasing team has a signed letter of intent conditional on removing one interior column for an open floor plan. Sales wants a same-day yes. The column sits on the standard grid; the structural drawings are at CD. Nobody has asked the structural engineer yet.

options.label: Walk the tributary math yourself today (spacing² × psf — it's a 30-ton question), then get the EOR to price the transfer structure and its schedule hit BEFORE responding to the tenant
options.outcome: The tributary arithmetic takes five minutes and reframes the conversation from 'remove a post' to 'buy a transfer beam.' The EOR's price makes the tenant decision honest — sometimes worth it for an anchor tenant, never worth it unpriced.

options.label: Say yes — engineers solve these things
options.outcome: Engineers do solve it: with a transfer beam at CD-stage change multipliers (M11's 3–5x), a deeper structure that eats ceiling height, and a schedule hit — all discovered after the yes, priced by the party with no alternative left.

options.label: Refuse — the grid is the grid
options.outcome: Structurally tidy, commercially lazy: transfer structures are bought all the time when the tenant math justifies them. A no without a price is as unexamined as a yes without one.

decisionPoints.debrief: The tributary check is the manager's superpower: five minutes of pizza-slice arithmetic tells you whether a request is trivial or a 30-ton engineering purchase — BEFORE anyone promises anything. Loads don't disappear; they get re-routed, and re-routing is priced. (V3-1)
